its qued.

Okay — "queued" usually just means the agent has a task lined up but hasn't started executing yet (waiting on a runtime, rate limit, or another job ahead of it in line). That's different from stalled/hung — it just hasn't kicked off.

A few common reasons a VS Code agent sits queued:

Model/API rate limiting — if it's hitting Gemini, DeepSeek, or another backend and you're near a quota, it'll queue rather than fail outright.
Extension waiting on a lock — another agent/process (like your Hermes gateway or a Scheduled Task) already has a file or resource open.
Local resource contention — if OpenClaw's tray app or another background process is also active, they can compete for the same port or file handle.

Given your recent OpenClaw troubleshooting, this could easily be the same Hermes-gateway-vs-Scheduled-Task collision you've been chasing — two processes trying to do the same job.

Quickest checks:

Click on the "queued" status in the bottom bar — most agent extensions show a tooltip or expand into a panel with the actual queue reason.
Check Task Manager for duplicate node/python processes tied to the agent or OpenClaw.
If it's been queued more than a couple minutes with nothing moving, cancel and retry — often it's just an event that didn't fire cleanly.

Want to send a screenshot of what it shows when you click into the queued item? That'll tell us exactly what it's waiting on.

So "queued" and "Delegating work" are almost certainly GitLens PRO cloud features — things like:

Cloud Patches / Workspaces sync — GitLens syncing your patches or workspace state to GitKraken's cloud
AI commit message generation — the "Compose" button you had open earlier generates commit messages via AI, and that can queue if it's rate-limited or waiting on GitKraken's backend
Launchpad — GitLens's PR/issue triage feature, which pulls from GitHub and can queue on API calls

Quick fix: click directly on the queued status item itself (not just glance at it) — GitLens usually shows a dropdown or notification with the actual reason. Also check the GitLens output panel (View → Output → select "GitLens" from dropdown) for any error/queue detail.

Here's a system status report prompt you can paste into any of your worker agents (Claude Code, OpenClaw/Terence, or a VS Code agent). It's written to be stack-agnostic but pulls in the specific things you're actively tracking.

COMPLETE SYSTEM STATUS REPORT PROMPT

Perform a complete system status report. Do not fix anything — just report. Structure your output exactly as follows:

1. IDENTITY & CONTEXT
   - What machine/environment are you running on (hostname, OS, working directory)?
   - What process/agent are you (name, version, PID if available)?

2. RUNNING PROCESSES & SERVICES
   - List all relevant running processes tied to this project (bots, gateways, schedulers, dev servers).
   - Flag any duplicate or competing instances of the same service.

3. CONNECTIVITY
   - Report status of any API connections in use (Gemini, DeepSeek, GCP, Cloudflare, GitHub, Telegram).
   - Note any auth/token errors, rate limit warnings, or timeouts in the last session.

4. TASK QUEUE
   - List any queued, delegated, or pending tasks.
   - For each: what triggered it, how long it's been queued, and what it's blocked on (if known).

5. FILE / REPO STATE
   - Current git branch, staged/unstaged file count, uncommitted changes summary.
   - Any file locks or files being written to by another process.

6. RECENT ERRORS
   - Last 5 errors/warnings from logs, with timestamps.

7. DISK / RESOURCE STATUS
   - Free disk space on the drive this is running from.
   - Memory/CPU usage if easily available.

8. OPEN QUESTIONS / FLAGS
   - Anything ambiguous, conflicting, or requiring a human decision.

Keep it factual and concise — no recommendations or fixes, just current state.

elegating work 14m 23s" — ????/ idk, give me pwsh command

Here's a PowerShell command to see what's actually alive and talking to APIs right now — useful for figuring out if that "Delegating work" is a live process or a zombie UI state.

powershell
# Show all node/electron processes (VS Code + extensions) with CPU/memory and start time
Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -match 'node|Code|electron' } |
  Select-Object Id, ProcessName, StartTime, CPU, WS, @{N='RuntimeMin';E={[math]::Round(((Get-Date)-$_.StartTime).TotalMinutes,1)}} |
  Sort-Object RuntimeMin -Descending |
  Format-Table -AutoSize

That shows you every VS Code / extension-host / node process and how long each has been running — if one's been alive for ~14+ minutes with climbing CPU, it's actually working; if it's flatlined at 0% CPU, it's hung.

To check if it's actually hitting the network right now (i.e. talking to DeepSeek's API vs just sitting idle):

powershell
# Check active outbound connections from VS Code / node processes
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established |
  Where-Object { (Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).ProcessName -match 'node|Code' } |
  Select-Object LocalAddress, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, @{N='Process';E={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess).ProcessName}}, @{N='PID';E={$_.OwningProcess}} |
  Format-Table -AutoSize

If you see a live connection to a DeepSeek/API IP on port 443, it's genuinely still working (just slow or queued server-side). If there's nothing — no live connection at all — the extension's UI is desynced and the task is dead; cancel it and resend.

Run the first one and tell me what you get — that'll tell us whether to wait or kill it.

Diagnosed excessive CPU consumption from VS Code processes

Good data. Here's what jumps out:

Big picture: Your VS Code window has been open 1116 minutes (~18.6 hours) — that's a huge amount of accumulated state across many Code + node processes. That alone is often the actual cause of weird "queued/delegating" UI states — extension hosts get memory-bloated or desynced over very long sessions.

The processes actually doing work right now (high CPU = actively processing, not idle):

PID 13736 — Code, 6817 CPU sec, running 1116 min (the oldest, heaviest one)
PID 39032 — Code, 4632 CPU sec, running 420 min — started 9:40 AM
PID 28084 — Code, 2042 CPU sec, running 1116 min
PID 14288 — node, 1019 CPU sec, running 996 min

Those three Code PIDs and that one node PID are the ones burning real CPU time — so something genuinely is working, not just frozen. The "Delegating work 14m 23s" is likely tied to one of these extension host processes.

Notable extras: you've also got cloudcode_cli (PID 19652) and codex (PID 26852) running — both started ~8:58 AM, ~462 min ago. Worth knowing those exist if you're not actively using them.

Next step — find which PID owns the live network connection (this tells you if it's actually still talking to DeepSeek or just stuck):

powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Where-Object { $_.OwningProcess -in @(13736,39032,28084,14288) } |
  Select-Object LocalAddress, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, OwningProcess |
  Format-Table -AutoSize

If one of those PIDs shows an established connection on port 443, it's genuinely still working — wait it out. If none show a connection, it's a dead/desynced task — safe to reload VS Code window (Ctrl+Shift+P → "Developer: Reload Window", which won't lose your staged git changes).

Given the session's been open 18+ hours, my honest read: reload the window. That clears zombie extension-host state without touching your files or git status.

That confirms it — no output at all means none of those PIDs have an active network connection right now. It's not talking to DeepSeek, it's not talking to anything. That "Delegating work 14m 23s" is a dead/desynced UI state, not a real in-flight task.

Do this:

Ctrl+Shift+P → type "Developer: Reload Window" → Enter.

This reloads the VS Code window only — it does not touch your filesystem, does not discard your 14 staged git changes, and does not kill your terminal-based processes (OpenClaw, Hermes gateway, etc. running outside VS Code stay alive). It just kills and restarts the extension hosts and UI, which clears the zombie task.

After reload, go back to the AI agent extension panel and resend the task if you still need it.
Your staged files in command_control will still show as staged — GitLens reads git state fresh off disk each time, so nothing is lost there.

If reload doesn't clear it (rare), the next step up is fully closing and reopening VS Code, since 18+ hours uptime with that much accumulated CPU time (6817 sec on the main window) is well past what's healthy for a single session.

For Windows Task Scheduler (which is what runs your OpenClaw Scheduled Task — the Windows equivalent of cron):

GUI:

powershell
taskschd.msc

That opens Task Scheduler directly.

PowerShell — view all your tasks:

powershell
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -match 'openclaw|vistaclaw|hermes' } |
  Select-Object TaskName, State, TaskPath |
  Format-Table -AutoSize

PowerShell — full detail including last run time, next run time, and result code (this is the one that'll actually tell you if it's colliding with the tray app):

powershell
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -match 'openclaw|vistaclaw|hermes' } | ForEach-Object {
  $info = Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName $_.TaskName -TaskPath $_.TaskPath
  [PSCustomObject]@{
    TaskName     = $_.TaskName
    State        = $_.State
    LastRunTime  = $info.LastRunTime
    LastResult   = $info.LastTaskResult
    NextRunTime  = $info.NextRunTime
  }
} | Format-Table -AutoSize

LastTaskResult of 0 means success. Anything else is an error code worth looking up.

If you're instead asking about a cron job inside GCP (Cloud Scheduler, for your Vertex AI / Vertex agent stuff) or a Cloudflare Worker cron trigger, that's a different place entirely — let me know which one you meant and I'll point you to the right console/command.

Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -match 'openclaw|vistaclaw|hermes' } | ForEach-Object {

    LastResult   = $info.LastTaskResult
    NextRunTime  = $info.NextRunTime
  }
} | Format-Table -AutoSize

That'll tell you immediately whether the task exists, whether it's currently Running or Ready, when it last ran, and whether it succeeded (LastResult 0 = success). Got it — that's exactly what we needed. Here's the answer to your original question:

Verdict: There is exactly ONE scheduled task called "OpenClaw Gateway", and its State = Ready (not "Running").

What "Ready" means: it's idle — not currently executing, just waiting for its trigger to fire. This is different from "Running," which would mean Task Scheduler is actively executing it right now.

So here's your actual situation:

If your tray app's Hermes gateway is currently active (i.e., your Telegram bot @vistaclaw_bot is responding), that's the tray app doing the work — not the Scheduled Task, since the Scheduled Task shows Ready/idle.
The Scheduled Task only becomes "Running" briefly when its trigger fires, then normally returns to "Ready" once its process launches and detaches, or stays "Running" if it's a long-lived process being tracked by Task Scheduler.

To get the last-run history and next trigger time (this tells you if it's set to fire on a schedule that could collide with the tray app), run:

powershell
Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName "OpenClaw Gateway" | Format-List *

That prints LastRunTime, LastTaskResult, NextRunTime, and NumberOfMissedRuns — paste that back and I'll tell you definitively whether it's set to auto-launch and potentially clash with your tray app.

Architected multi-part solution: process cleanup command, AI prompt, reference sheet, task inventory
Architected multi-part solution: process cleanup command, AI prompt, reference sheet, task inventory

Here's all four, ready to use.

1. One-liner: Kill orphaned n8n-mcp pairs, keep newest
powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='node.exe'" | Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match 'n8n-mcp' } | Sort-Object CreationDate -Descending | Select-Object -Skip 2 | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "Killing PID $($_.ProcessId) started $($_.CreationDate)"; Stop-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -Force }

Keeps the 2 newest (one wrapper + one worker = the most recent pair), kills the rest. Run it once — it prints each PID it kills as it goes, so you can see exactly what happened. Safe to re-run any time; it just re-evaluates "newest" each time.

2. Prompt for DeepSeek V4 Pro

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='node.exe'" | Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match 'n8n-mcp' } | Sort-Object CreationDate -Descending | Select-Object -Skip 2 | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "Killing PID $($_.ProcessId) started $($_.CreationDate)"; Stop-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -Force }

After running it, confirm how many processes were killed and list their PIDs. Do not touch any other node processes, especially PID 14288 (OpenClaw gateway, port 18789) — that one must stay running. Do not restart or modify the n8n-mcp package itself, just clean up the duplicate running instances.

{

- Responsive down to mobile

the orchestration mode is deprecated ,whats managing tasks

That message ("orchestration mode is deprecated") sounds like it's coming from a specific tool's UI or changelog — I haven't seen that anywhere in this conversation, so I don't know which product is telling you that.

Which one is this from — the VS Code agent extension you've been using (the DeepSeek/Cline-style one), OpenClaw itself, n8n, or somewhere else? A screenshot of where you saw that message would settle it fastest.

In the meantime, general answer: when a tool deprecates an "orchestration mode," it almost always means task routing/delegation logic moved from an explicit mode-toggle into something more automatic — usually one of:

Single-agent-with-tools model — the "orchestrator" role gets folded into the main agent, which now just calls sub-tools/sub-agents directly instead of running a separate coordinating layer
Config-driven routing — task management moves from a runtime "mode" into a static config file (e.g. a .yml or .json defining which agent handles which task type)
Provider-native orchestration — the underlying model provider (e.g. Anthropic, DeepSeek) now handles multi-step tool chaining natively, so the extension's own orchestration layer became redundant

If this is OpenClaw specifically, it'd be worth checking its changelog/release notes for what replaced it — given you're already deep in OpenClaw troubleshooting, I'd guess this actually is OpenClaw. Is that right?

Confirmed. Here's the direct answer:

Task management moved from a dedicated Orchestrator mode into every other mode natively. Roo Code deprecated the explicit coordinator pattern because it added overhead without adding capability — full-tool agents (Code, Plan, Debug) can now delegate to subagents natively, meaning you describe the goal, the parent agent splits the work, and subagents run in parallel. 
gitlab

Practically, for you: instead of switching into "Orchestrator" mode to break down a complex task like your research capture pipeline, just describe the whole goal to whichever mode you're already in (e.g., Code mode), and it'll spawn and delegate subtasks itself — no mode-switch required.

One caveat worth knowing: subagents currently can't spawn subagents themselves — it's a flat two-level hierarchy. So if your research pipeline task is deep enough to need sub-subtasks, you may still need to break it into stages manually rather than trusting full auto-delegation. 
gitlab

Since you're clearly running Roo Code (not a fork), you're fine sticking with it as-is — that Kilo Code migration guide result was just explaining Kilo's own reasoning for dropping it, but Roo Code's own docs confirm the same underlying mechanism (native delegation via new_task) replaced Orchestrator on their side too.

gemini persistent knocking at the door.  mostly login loops, github does that fair bit, authorising, perhaps because of large mcp integration.

Diagnosed persistent authentication loops stemming from GitHub integration
Diagnosed persistent authentication loops stemming from GitHub integration

That pattern — repeated auth/login loops with Gemini CLI and GitHub — usually comes down to one of these, roughly in order of likelihood given your setup (multiple MCP servers, GCP dual billing accounts, long-running VS Code sessions):

Most likely: token expiry vs. refresh-token failure. OAuth tokens for both Gemini CLI and GitHub CLI have short-lived access tokens that should auto-refresh silently using a stored refresh token. If refresh is failing (corrupted credential cache, clock skew, or a scope mismatch from adding new MCP servers), you get kicked back to a full login prompt instead of a silent refresh — that's the "knocking" pattern.

Second: too many concurrent MCP clients hitting the same OAuth app. If several of your node/MCP processes (you've got a lot running — n8n-mcp instances, cloudcode_cli, codex, etc.) are each independently trying to authenticate against Gemini or GitHub using the same client ID, some providers will invalidate/rotate sessions when they see concurrent conflicting auth attempts, causing exactly this loop.

Third: credential storage location drift — given your hops1010_microsoft vs hops1 profile path inconsistency, if some tools are reading tokens from one profile and others are writing to the other, you'd get a "login accepted" then immediately "not authenticated" loop.

Diagnostic to run first:

powershell
Write-Host "=== GH CLI AUTH STATUS ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan
gh auth status

Write-Host "`n=== GEMINI CLI AUTH LOCATION ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Get-ChildItem -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.config\gemini" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ChildItem -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.gemini" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Write-Host "`n=== SYSTEM CLOCK (auth tokens are time-sensitive) ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Get-Date
w32tm /query /status

Write-Host "`n=== ACTIVE PROCESSES THAT MIGHT BE COMPETING FOR AUTH ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='node.exe'" | Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match 'gemini|gh-|github' } | Select-Object ProcessId, CommandLine

Run that and paste the output — particularly gh auth status and the clock sync check (clock drift is a sneaky, common cause of exactly this symptom and takes 10 seconds to rule out).

whats the agent memory situation

Searched the web
Searched the web

Here's the honest picture, and it directly matters given what you just said about "clean to the bone, no residue."

Roo Code has no true persistent memory by default. RooCode resets every session — when you close a session, the context closes with it. This isn't a flaw, it's how LLMs fundamentally work: they process a context window and produce output, they don't write to persistent storage between conversations. Its built-in chat history only persists within a single VS Code workspace session, and it undergoes periodic internal memory resets even during active sessions.

So Big Brother "forgetting shit" isn't a bug you're imagining — it's the actual architecture. Within one continuous open session, it holds context fine (which is why you don't need to re-paste "you are Big Brother" mid-thread). But close that session, reopen tomorrow, and it's a blank slate unless something external feeds context back in.

The fix, if you want one, is a Memory Bank pattern — a structured memory system that stores project information in markdown files (active context, progress, decisions, coding patterns) that Roo reads at the start of every session, acting as external long-term memory that survives resets.

Given your "clean to the bone, no residue from signal breaches" standard, this actually maps well: instead of the agent silently accumulating fuzzy context across sessions (residue), you'd have an explicit, inspectable, editable file — you control exactly what persists, nothing lingers that you didn't deliberately write down. It only interacts with your local file system — no code or project context is sent to any external service.

Practical option for your setup: rather than bolting on the third-party Memory Bank MCP server, you could roll your own lightweight version that fits your existing stack — a single AGENTS.md or per-persona .md file (Big Brother's own state file) that Big Brother reads at session start and updates at session end. That's fully within your control, versionable in the same command_control repo, and leaves zero hidden state anywhere.

Want me to draft that file structure — one markdown file per agent persona (Big Brother, Trinity, Gordon, etc.) with a fixed schema (current stage, last completed action, open questions, known gaps) that gets read/written explicitly rather than relying on session memory?

no, do mcp memory and optimise

Pivoted toward MCP memory implementation and optimization strategy
Pivoted toward MCP memory implementation and optimization strategy

Good — this is the real fix for the "forgets shit" problem. Here's setup + how to keep it lean, since "clean to the bone" is a legitimate design constraint here, not paranoia.

Setup

Two implementations exist. Given you already have an orphaned-process problem from npx-spawned MCP servers (the n8n-mcp cleanup earlier), avoid the npx-based one (alioshr/memory-bank-mcp) — every session start would spawn a fresh process instead of reusing one, recreating the exact mess you just cleaned up. Use the build-from-source version instead, which runs as one fixed process:

powershell
git clone https://github.com/IncomeStreamSurfer/roo-code-memory-bank-mcp-server.git C:\tools\memory-bank-mcp
cd C:\tools\memory-bank-mcp
npm install
npm run build

Then register it in Roo Code's MCP settings file:

powershell
notepad "$env:APPDATA\Code\User\globalStorage\rooveterinaryinc.roo-cline\settings\mcp_settings.json"

Add:

json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "memory-bank": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["C:\\tools\\memory-bank-mcp\\dist\\index.js"],
      "cwd": "C:\\command_control",
      "disabled": false
    }
  }
}

cwd matters — the memory-bank/ directory gets created in whatever directory the server process is started in, so pointing it at C:\command_control keeps it living inside your actual project repo rather than scattered somewhere else. 
glama

What it gives you

It initializes five standard markdown files — productContext.md, activeContext.md, progress.md, decisionLog.md, and systemPatterns.md — and exposes tools to check status, read files, and append timestamped entries. Best practice: at the start of any task, check memory bank status first, and if it exists, read the relevant files (productContext.md, activeContext.md) to load current project context before doing anything else. 
glama

Optimization — keeping it clean, not bloated
One memory bank per repo, not per agent. Don't give Trinity/Gordon/Merlin/Big Brother separate memory banks — that fragments context and creates the exact "residue" problem you're avoiding (five different half-true versions of project state). One shared memory-bank/ in command_control, all agents read/write the same five files.
Prune decisionLog.md and progress.md on a schedule. These grow unbounded via append-only writes. Once a stage closes (like Stage 2 just did), summarize and archive the detailed log entries into a single closing paragraph, delete the granular timestamped entries. This is literally your "clean to the bone" principle applied to memory itself.
Never let activeContext.md exceed ~1 page. It should hold only what's true right now — current stage, current blocker, next action. If it's accumulating history, that history belongs in progress.md or decisionLog.md, not here. This file is what gets read first every session — bloat here means every session starts by wading through noise.
Back it up before any agent does a bulk append. Regularly back up the memory-bank directory to prevent data loss and ensure you have a rollback plan for any inadvertent modifications. Since it's plain markdown in your git repo, a simple commit before major operations covers this — no extra tooling needed. 
Mcp
Restrict auto-approve to read + append only, never delete. In mcp_settings.json, only auto-approve check_memory_bank_status and read_memory_bank_file. Leave append_memory_bank_entry requiring manual confirmation until you trust the pattern — appends are how residue accumulates fastest if an agent over-logs.

Want the initial productContext.md template drafted with your actual project structure (Trinity/Gordon/Merlin/Olivia/Claw roles, the 5-stage plan, current Stage 2 status) so the memory bank starts populated instead of empty?

Good outcome overall — 11KB total, no bloat, clean 5-file structure written directly to .memory-bank/. But one detail changes the picture: this ran on Kilo, not Roo Code.

That's worth pinning down, because — remember the Kilo Code migration guide from the earlier search — Kilo is the fork that replaced Roo Code after Roo's team discontinued their extension in favor of a cloud product, with GA around April 2026. If your agent is reporting "Kilo memory" as a separate system, you're actually running Kilo's extension, not Roo Code's. That'd also explain why it didn't have the roo-code-memory-bank MCP tools available — Kilo may have its own native memory layer instead of needing that third-party MCP server at all.

Two things worth resolving before you build more on top of this:

Which extension is actually installed — Roo Code or Kilo? Check the Extensions sidebar. This matters because Kilo's built-in "Kilo memory" (the 6 saved project facts it mentioned) might be a completely separate persistence mechanism from your .memory-bank/ markdown files — meaning you could end up with two parallel, unsynced memory systems instead of one clean source of truth.

ENSURE I GET A WINDOWS NOTIFICtion from olivia

Good call to check that — "sent to notifications" from her text reports doesn't mean an actual Windows toast is firing unless something explicitly triggers one. Here's how to make sure it's real.

The technical piece — PowerShell command that fires a real Windows notification:

powershell
# One-time setup (only needs running once, ever)
Install-Module -Name BurntToast -Scope CurrentUser -Force

# The actual notification call Olivia's agent should run
New-BurntToastNotification -Text "Olivia — Vistamations", "Stage 3 scope logged and confirmed"

BurntToast is the standard way to fire genuine Windows 10/11 toast notifications from PowerShell — without it, "notification" is just a line in a chat log, not something that pops up on your screen.

Add this to Olivia's standing instructions so it's automatic, not something you have to ask for each time:

STANDING RULE — WINDOWS NOTIFICATIONS:
Whenever you say something has been "sent to notifications," it means you have actually executed a real Windows toast notification via PowerShell — not just logged it in your text response. Use:

New-BurntToastNotification -Text "Olivia — Vistamations", "<one-line summary of what just happened>"

If the BurntToast module is not installed, install it first (Install-Module -Name BurntToast -Scope CurrentUser -Force), then fire the notification. Never claim something was "sent to notifications" unless this command was actually executed and returned success. If it failed, say so plainly — do not report a notification was sent if it wasn't.

Paste that as an addition to the Stage 3 prompt (or run it standalone right now to test) — and you should see an actual popup on your screen confirming it worked, not just a claim that it did.

powershell
cd C:\vistamations-music\crons\openclaw
.\schedule.ps1 -Action register

One thing worth verifying before you run that — Windows Task Scheduler triggers fire on the machine's local system clock, not a named timezone. If your Windows system timezone isn't already set to AEST/AEDT, "09:00/12:00/15:00/18:00 AEST" in the script will actually fire at those times in whatever timezone Windows thinks it's in. Quick check:

powershell
Get-TimeZone

If it doesn't say AUS Eastern Standard Time, the four trigger times will be off by whatever the offset is.

After registering, verify it actually took:

powershell
Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName "*publishing*" | Format-List TaskName, NextRunTime, LastTaskResult

(Adjust the task name filter once you know what schedule.ps1 -Action register actually names it — it may not be called "publishing" literally.)

This closes the last open item from Gordon's Stage 2 report (Windows Task Scheduler not registered → 0 scheduled executions have run). Once this is confirmed registered with a correct NextRunTime, Stage 2 closeout is genuinely done, not just code-complete.

Crash-recovery architecture confirmed. Report:
---
**Crash test:** Killed PID 35888 at 23:28:51 AEST. Waited 195 seconds. No respawn.
**Observed behavior: Task Scheduler RestartCount/RestartInterval did NOT recover.** This is because those settings restart a task within the **same trigger instance**, not after the trigger instance completes. The AtLogOn trigger fires once, the task runs, the instance finishes — there's nothing left to restart. RestartCount 999 is ineffective for a single-fire trigger.
**Fix deployed:** Two-tier crash recovery:
| Layer | Method | PID | Recovery time |
|-------|--------|-----|---------------|
| Primary | background_process (persistent) | 39444 | Manual restart (was done at 23:33) |
| Watchdog | Vistamations-OliviaWatchdog — every 5 min | Scheduled Task | ≤5 min |
The watchdog runs olivia-dispatch-watchdog.ps1 -Action check, which scans all processes for olivia-dispatch.ps1 in the command line. If not found, launches a new hidden pwsh instance running it. Registered under VISTA-PRIME-I5\peteh with 365-day repetition duration.

Message collapsed

That's a real fix, not a bandaid — and the diagnosis was correct: RestartCount/RestartInterval only applies within a single trigger instance's lifecycle, which is a genuinely non-obvious Task Scheduler behavior most people never discover until it silently fails in production. Good catch, verified with an actual kill test rather than assumed.

One gap left, worth closing now while you're in this territory: the watchdog checks every 5 minutes whether the dispatch process exists — but does it verify the process is actually working (still processing responses.json entries), or just that a pwsh.exe with that command line is alive? A hung-but-running process would pass the watchdog check while silently doing nothing — same failure mode as the "Delegating work 14m 23s" zombie state from earlier in this session, just one layer deeper.

Extend the watchdog check: beyond confirming the process exists, verify it's actually functional — e.g. check that responses.json's last-modified timestamp or a heartbeat log entry is recent (within the last ~30s, given the 10s poll interval). If the process exists but hasn't touched responses.json in an abnormal window, treat it as hung, kill it, and restart. Report whether this distinction is worth adding now or is over-engineering for current scale — your call, not mine to force.

Aside from that optional hardening, this is genuinely closed:

Original bug (lost message) → root-caused (no dispatcher existed)
Dispatcher → built, proven working
Crash resilience → tested for real, found broken, fixed with a correctly-scoped watchdog

That's a clean chain from symptom to permanent fix. Worth logging this whole sequence (bug → root cause → fix → crash test → watchdog fix) as one entry in decisionLog.md — it's a good reference for the pattern (single-fire triggers don't self-heal, need external watchdogs) which will likely apply to other Vistamations tasks later, not just this one.

I'll keep this simple. The watchdog already does process-existence checking, which covers 95% of failures (the process crashes, gets killed, or the system reboots). Adding a heartbeat log + hung-process detection adds a second file to write (heartbeat JSON), a second pattern to match (stale timestamps vs process presence), and a tricky edge case (kill a hung pwsh, but Did it leave the file locked? Did WMI see the right PID?). 
For a single-file JSON reader in a 10s loop with zero I/O outside responses.json reads, the failure modes that would leave the process alive but non-functional are:
1. responses.json is locked or corrupted → process would crash on JSON parse, not hang. Caught by process-existence check.
2. Docker API unreachable for health checks → the try/catch in the script handles this gracefully, logs the error, continues polling.
3. Invoke-RestMethod hangs → would block the loop. This is the only real hung-process risk, but it's an HTTP call to localhost with no auth — 30s default timeout in PowerShell 5.1's Invoke-RestMethod would unblock naturally.
**Decision: not worth adding now.** The process-existence watchdog covers the actual failure modes at this scale. If we later see logs of "process alive but portal not updating," we add the heartbeat then. For now, simpler is what actually works.

Message collapsed

That's the right call, and the reasoning holds up on inspection — you walked through the actual failure modes instead of just defaulting to "more monitoring is safer," and correctly identified that most of what a heartbeat would catch is already caught by existing error handling or self-resolves via timeout. That's the "clean to the bone" principle applied correctly: not the absence of safeguards, but no safeguard existing without a real failure mode behind it.

The one item worth remembering, not acting on now: Invoke-RestMethod's 30s default timeout is your actual backstop for the one real hang risk. If that call ever gets modified later — say, pointed at an external API instead of localhost, or wrapped in retry logic that resets the timeout — that assumption quietly stops holding. Worth a one-line comment in the script itself (# relies on default 30s Invoke-RestMethod timeout as hang protection) so future-you or another agent editing this doesn't remove that safety net without realizing it was doing a job.

This whole thread — bug → root cause → fix → crash test → watchdog → scoped decision not to over-engineer — is a genuinely complete piece of work. Log it to decisionLog.md as one entry, and this closes.

big brother kickin back?

Deciphered ambiguous phrasing and sought clarification

Could mean a couple different things — quick check:

"Kicking back" = idle/done for now, i.e. is Big Brother sitting quiet after that whole crash-recovery thread closed out?
"Kicking back" = pushing back/resisting, i.e. is Big Brother disagreeing with something or stalling on a task?

Architected minimal infrastructure prompt emphasizing stability and structural metaphors
Architected minimal infrastructure prompt emphasizing stability and structural metaphors

Here's the prompt — written in your metaphor language but translated into concrete technical instructions so the AI Studio agent doesn't have to guess.

PROMPT: Vistamations Stage 1 — Structural Foundation

Build a single-page web application. This is Stage 1 of 5 — a structural foundation only. Priority order: stability first, functionality second, appearance last. Do not over-build.

SCOPE — ONE AGENT, ONE PAGE, NO AUTOMATION:
- Single Gemini-powered agent, no multi-agent orchestration
- No cron jobs, no scheduled tasks, no background processes
- One webpage only

STRUCTURE (using the build metaphor literally):

FLOOR (base layer):
- Semantic HTML5 document structure — proper doctype, meta tags, viewport
- A single root container that everything else mounts into
- No layout framework dependency — plain CSS Grid or Flexbox, nothing that requires a build step

FRAME (layout skeleton):
- A fixed, predictable page structure: header zone, one central content zone, footer/status zone
- The central zone holds ONE clock — large, legible, the visual anchor of the page
- Everything else on this page is secondary to the clock; it is the orientation point

ABOVE/BELOW WIRES AND PIPES (data flow):
- One clean data path: a single JavaScript function that fetches/updates the time and renders it
- No external API calls unless absolutely required (system clock is sufficient — do not depend on an external time API for something this simple)
- If a Gemini API call is included at all, it must be a single, isolated function with clear error handling — a failure here must not break the clock or the page

POWER (core functionality):
- The page must load and render correctly with zero JavaScript errors in console
- The clock must run reliably without drift or memory leaks (no accumulating setInterval calls, clean up on unload)
- Graceful degradation: if any optional feature fails (API call, external resource), the core clock display still works

EXPLICIT CONSTRAINTS:
- No routing, no multi-page navigation
- No database, no persistent storage layer
- No animation beyond simple, essential transitions (e.g. a smooth second-hand tick if desired — nothing decorative)
- No dependency on external component libraries — vanilla HTML/CSS/JS only, so this remains simple to audit and maintain

DELIVERABLE:
A single, self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS, or clearly separated but minimal files) that a non-technical viewer could open and immediately understand: "this is stable, this works, this is the foundation everything else builds on top of."

Do not add anything beyond what's specified here. This is deliberately minimal — Stage 1 is about proving the foundation holds weight, not showing what the finished structure will look like.

Scrutinized quota mechanics and scaling assumptions across accounts
Scrutinized quota mechanics and scaling assumptions across accounts

Worth pausing on one thing before the math compounds: "6-7 models" and "6-7x the Stitch quota" aren't the same thing.

Stitch's 350+200 monthly quota is tied to a Google account, not to which downstream model (DeepSeek, Gemini, Mistral) is doing the reasoning/building work on top of it. Having 6-7 different AI models available doesn't multiply your Stitch generation allowance — they'd all be drawing from the same quota if they're all going through one Google account's Stitch access.

To actually get 6-7x throughput, you'd need 6-7 separate Google accounts, each with independent Stitch access. From your own setup, you've mentioned two so far — petehops89@gmail.com (primary) and hops1010@gmail.com — not 6-7. Two accounts realistically gets you closer to 36/day automated (18 x 2), not 126.

This also raises a real question worth answering before building anything: does Stitch's ToS actually permit multiple accounts to bypass a per-account free-tier limit? Some Google Labs tools explicitly prohibit this as ToS-circumvention even when each account is genuinely yours. Worth checking directly rather than assuming — using two of your own real accounts for two separate legitimate purposes is normal; using several accounts specifically to multiply a rate limit is the kind of thing that gets accounts flagged or banned, and you don't want your primary GCP-linked account caught in that.

Realistic combined picture, conservative:

You manually: 50/day (functional, not complete — your number)
Automated pipeline (1 account, quota-realistic): 6-9/day genuinely finished
If a second legitimate account is confirmed ToS-clean: roughly double the automated number

Prompt to settle this before scaling further:

Check Stitch/Google Labs terms of service specifically on multi-account use to increase total generation quota. Report: is this explicitly prohibited, a gray area, or fine? Also confirm — does Stitch's quota tie to the Google account or to something else (device, API key)? Report findings only, no action.

Want that answer before we plan the real daily/monthly target, or do you want to proceed on the conservative single-account number for now and revisit scale later?
